**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section » (quatre questions au total, au moins une par section ; trois sections de deux questions : Section One 1-2, Section Two 3-4, Section Three 5-6). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question : Q5 = 5 + (2 x 2) + 3 + 4 + 4 + 5 = 25 ; Q6 = 5 + (2 x 2) + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25. Aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé. La page de garde de 2024 ne donne pas de barème par partie pour les dissertations (contrairement à 2022) : les titres « (5 marks) », « (7 marks) »... des corrigés de dissertation ne sont donc pas utilisés, seule la structure exigée (problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse, conclusion) est suivie.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), code 0790, JUNE 2024, trois heures.

Q4 : le sujet dit « The communalistic spirit dominates the African ethical worldview. Discuss ». Attributions : Mbiti (« I am because we are... »), Menkiti (la personnalité s'acquiert par l'incorporation dans la communauté), Gyekye (communautarisme modéré, critique de Menkiti), Senghor, Nyerere (Ujamaa), Kaunda (humanisme), Oruka (sages) : positions connues, sans citation littérale hormis la formule de Mbiti, sans date ni titre d'ouvrage.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The communalistic spirit dominates the African ethical worldview. Discuss

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction and problematic.** Ethics concerns the values and norms that guide conduct. A common claim in African philosophy is that African moral thought is communal: the group comes first, and moral value is defined by one's relation to others. The question asks whether the spirit of community *dominates* the African ethical worldview. The problem is to decide whether communalism is really the central and overriding principle of African ethics, or whether it is one principle among others, and whether it leaves any place for the individual.

**Thesis: communalism dominates African ethics.**
- *The person is defined by the community.* John Mbiti summed it up: "I am because we are, and since we are, therefore I am". The individual exists and becomes a moral being through others. Ifeanyi Menkiti argues that in African thought personhood is *acquired* gradually, through incorporation into the community and the fulfilment of its obligations; the community comes before the individual, ontologically and morally.
- *Ubuntu.* In Southern Africa, "a person is a person through other persons": virtues such as solidarity, hospitality, compassion, sharing and respect for elders are the core of moral life, and the aim of morality is harmony of the group.
- *Political and social expression.* Senghor spoke of the community-based character of African society, and of a socialism founded on it; Julius Nyerere's *Ujamaa* (familyhood) and Kenneth Kaunda's humanism built an ethics and a policy on solidarity and mutual care; the extended family, the age-group, work in common, funerals and the sharing of wealth show the same spirit in practice.
- *Moral rules support the group.* Many traditional values (duty to elders, respect for the ancestors, sharing, reconciliation palaver) aim to preserve the unity of the group; morally good conduct is what builds the community, and immoral conduct is what destroys it.

**Antithesis: communalism does not dominate, or not alone.**
- *The individual also counts.* Kwame Gyekye argues that the radical communitarianism of Menkiti is inaccurate: Akan thought gives the individual a distinct moral worth, rationality, capacity for choice and responsibility, and rights. The person is both communal and autonomous, so a "moderate communitarianism" fits the evidence better. An ethic in which everything depends on the group would also make personal responsibility and conscience meaningless.
- *Danger of conformism and injustice.* A dominant communal spirit can suppress dissent, justify the pressure of the group on the person (e.g. on women, the young, minorities), favour nepotism or tribalism, and exclude outsiders.
- *Diversity and change.* Africa has many peoples and moral traditions, with other sources (religion, individual conscience, personal virtues, the sages of Oruka); modern urbanisation, schooling, markets and the nation-state have increased individualism, so that the claim of a unique, dominant spirit describes an ideal more than reality.
- *Idealisation.* Critics note that the picture of an "African communal ethic" may have been produced in reaction to Western individualism and may be simplified.

**Synthesis.** The communal spirit is a central and distinctive feature of African ethical thought, probably its most important organising value, but it does not exhaust it. The best account is a balance, as in Gyekye's moderate communitarianism: the community gives the person identity, values and duties, and the person keeps dignity, rights and responsibility. "Dominates" is therefore acceptable if it means "has priority in emphasis", not if it means "excludes individual value".

**Conclusion.** The statement is largely true as a description of the emphasis of African moral thought and practice, but too strong if taken to deny the individual. African ethics is communal in spirit while recognising the person as a responsible moral agent; the challenge today is to keep the solidarity of the community while protecting individual freedom and rights.
